content: Gunnera is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants, some of which are exceptionally large in size. This genus is the sole member of the family Gunneraceae. The species within this genus, numbering between 40 and 50, exhibit significant variation in leaf size, with some leaves reaching lengths of up to 5 meters (approximately 16 feet). Optimal germination occurs in conditions that are very moist but not waterlogged, with temperatures ranging from 22 to 29°C (72 to 84°F). One notable species, Gunnera masafuerae, native to the Juan Fernández Islands off the coast of Chile, is slightly smaller than the largest species. According to Skottsberg, its stems can reach a thickness of 5 inches. On the nearby Isla Más Afuera, this species can grow up to 5 meters (18 feet) in height, with stems 25–30 cm (10–12 inches) thick and leaves up to 2 meters (6 feet 4 inches) wide. Another remarkable species, Gunnera magnifica, found in the Colombian Andes, produces the largest leaf buds of any known plant, measuring up to 60 cm (2 feet) in length and 40 cm (16 inches) in thickness. Its leaves can grow to lengths of 2.7 meters (8 feet 10 inches), and its inflorescences can reach 3 meters (7 feet 6 inches) in length, weighing approximately 13 kilograms (29 pounds). Other giant Gunnera species are distributed throughout the Neotropics and Hawaii. In contrast, smaller species are found in New Zealand, such as Gunnera albocarpa, which has leaves only 1–2 cm long. Similarly, in South America, Gunnera magellanica has leaves measuring 5–9 cm wide on stalks 8–15 cm long. Commonly referred to as giant rhubarb, the genus Gunnera was named in honor of the Norwegian botanist Johann Ernst Gunnerus. Notable Species: Gunnera albocarpa Gunnera arenaria Gunnera densiflora Gunnera dentata Gunnera flavida Gunnera hamiltonii Gunnera kauaiensis Gunnera magellanica Gunnera magnifica Gunnera manicata Gunnera masafuerae Gunnera monoica Gunnera perpensa Gunnera petaloïdea Gunnera prorepens Gunnera tinctoria Cyanobacterial Symbiosis: In nature, all Gunnera plants form a symbiotic relationship with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria, believed to be exclusively Nostoc punctiforme. The bacteria enter the plant through specialized glands located at the base of each leaf stalk. This interaction results in an intracellular symbiosis, where the bacteria provide the plant with fixed nitrogen in exchange for fixed carbon from the plant. This unique intracellular relationship in higher plants offers potential insights into developing novel symbioses between crop plants and cyanobacteria, which could enable growth in soils deficient in fixed nitrogen. Uses: The stalks of Gunnera tinctoria (commonly known as nalcas) are edible and are primarily consumed fresh. They are also used in salads, as an ingredient in liquors, or to make marmalade. The leaves of this species are traditionally used to cover curanto, a traditional Chilean dish. In Southern Africa, Gunnera perpensa is utilized as a source of traditional medicine.
